In browser-commander 0.28.0, three things go wrong by default on macOS:\n\n1. **Chrome for Testing shows a bar over every page:** «Chrome for Testing v156.0.8078.4 is only for automated testing. For regular browsing, use a standard version of Chrome. [Download Chrome]». It takes vertical space in every window. `--disable-infobars` (the `no-infobars` restriction) does not remove it.\n2. **The user's Google Chrome is taken over:** `resolveLaunchExecutable()` prefers the installed Google Chrome (`channel: 'chrome'`). Started with another `--user-data-dir`, it is still the same app (`com.google.Chrome`) to macOS. When the user's own Chrome is not running, a click on Chrome in the Dock, ⌘T, or a link opened from another app goes to the automation window. An automation that keeps one tab then closes the user's tab.\n3. **The keychain is asked again and again:** Chrome for Testing started without `--use-mock-keychain` asks «Google Chrome for Testing wants to access key \"Chromium Safe Storage\" in your keychain» at each start.\n\n## Root cause and fix\n\n1. Chromium shows the Chrome for Testing bar unless `--test-type=gpu` is given. This is the only command-line value that skips it, from `chrome/browser/ui/startup/infobar_utils.cc`:\n   ```cpp\n   #if BUILDFLAG(CHROME_FOR_TESTING)\n   bool IsGpuTest() {\n     return base::CommandLine::ForCurrentProcess()->GetSwitchValueASCII(switches::kTestType) == \"gpu\";\n   }\n   #endif\n   ...\n   if (show_bad_flags_security_warnings) {\n   #if BUILDFLAG(CHROME_FOR_TESTING)\n     if (!IsGpuTest()) { ... ChromeForTestingInfoBarDelegate::Create(); }\n   #endif\n   ```\n   The only other way is the `CommandLineFlagSecurityWarningsEnabled` policy. `--test-type` also skips the later infobars (session crashed, default browser, …) and does not turn `navigator.webdriver` on.\n2. Launch Chrome for Testing (Playwright's or Puppeteer's), which is an app of its own (`com.google.chrome.for.testing`), and never the user's Google Chrome. The installed Google Chrome should be used only on request.\n3. Pass `--use-mock-keychain` to Chrome for Testing, so the keychain is never asked. Logins moved from a Google Chrome profile can be read by Google Chrome headless, which already has access to its own keychain entry, and then set with `Storage.setCookies`.\n\n## Requested\n\n- A default launch restriction `no-chrome-for-testing-infobar` (`--test-type=gpu`) whenever the executable is Chrome for Testing.\n- `resolveLaunchExecutable()` defaults to Chrome for Testing for automation, not to the user's Google Chrome.\n- `--use-mock-keychain` by default for Chrome for Testing.\n- Tests for each of these.\n\nThe hh-job-application-automation app works around this in `src/browser-session.mjs` (commit a868526 in konard/hh-job-application-automation).\n\n===== 180 Trace screenshots can leave a headful page stuck at its old size after a window resize\n## Problem\n\nA headful page that is being traced (`startTrace`, default `screenshots: 'checkpoints'`) can stop following its window size. After the user resizes the window, the page is still drawn at the old size in the top-left corner and the rest of the window stays blank. It stays that way until the page is reloaded.\n\nBy default, the browser must look and behave exactly like a real browser.\n\n## Cause\n\nThe trace recorder takes checkpoint screenshots with the engine's `page.screenshot({ type: 'png' })` (`src/traces/recorder.js`, `screenshot()`). For a viewport screenshot, Playwright 1.64 sends `Page.captureScreenshot` with a `clip` set to the current viewport. Chrome emulates the clip's size while it captures. If the window is resized during the capture, the emulated size can stay in place after the capture ends.\n\n## Reproduction\n\nMeasured with Chrome for Testing 156.0.8078.4 on macOS, Playwright 1.64, browser-commander 0.28 (0.32.1 has the same code):\n\n1. Start a headful Chrome and attach with `connectBrowser({ engine: 'playwright', cdpEndpoint })`.\n2. Keep taking screenshots in a loop while the window is resized in about 20 steps with `Browser.setWindowBounds`.\n3. Compare `innerWidth` with `outerWidth`.\n\n| Screenshot method | Drags where the page got stuck |\n|---|---|\n| `page.screenshot({ type: 'png' })` (Playwright) | 2 of 8 |\n| CDP `Page.captureScreenshot { format: 'png' }` (no clip) | 0 of 8 |\n| CDP `Page.captureScreenshot { fromSurface: false, captureBeyondViewport: false }` | 0 of 8 |\n| Trace checkpoints with the no-clip capture | 0 of 12 |\n\n## Suggested fix\n\nFor trace checkpoint screenshots, and any default capture of a page with no fixed viewport, use CDP `Page.captureScreenshot` without a `clip`. `captureStableViewport` already does this when `viewportSize()` is null.\n\nWorkaround in hh-job-application-automation: pass `startTrace` a `page` whose `screenshot` is the CDP capture without a clip.\nShell cwd was reset to /tmp/gh-issue-solver-resume-d85c9a23-5c61-45c3-b1e1-7d099f9ef893-1792597658851",

This is the only command-line value that skips it, from `chrome/browser/ui/startup/infobar_utils.cc`:\n   ```cpp\n   #if BUILDFLAG(CHROME_FOR_TESTING)\n   bool IsGpuTest() {\n     return base::CommandLine::ForCurrentProcess()->GetSwitchValueASCII(switches::kTestType) == \"gpu\";\n   }\n   #endif\n   ...\n   if (show_bad_flags_security_warnings) {\n   #if BUILDFLAG(CHROME_FOR_TESTING)\n     if (!IsGpuTest()) { ... ChromeForTestingInfoBarDelegate::Create(); }\n   #endif\n   ```\n   The only other way is the `CommandLineFlagSecurityWarningsEnabled` policy. `--test-type` also skips the later infobars (session crashed, default browser, …) and does not turn `navigator.webdriver` on.\n2. Launch Chrome for Testing (Playwright's or Puppeteer's), which is an app of its own (`com.google.chrome.for.testing`), and never the user's Google Chrome. The installed Google Chrome should be used only on request.\n3. Pass `--use-mock-keychain` to Chrome for Testing, so the keychain is never asked. Logins moved from a Google Chrome profile can be read by Google Chrome headless, which already has access to its own keychain entry, and then set with `Storage.setCookies`.\n\n## Requested\n\n- A default launch restriction `no-chrome-for-testing-infobar` (`--test-type=gpu`) whenever the executable is Chrome for Testing.\n- `resolveLaunchExecutable()` defaults to Chrome for Testing for automation, not to the user's Google Chrome.\n- `--use-mock-keychain` by default for Chrome for Testing.\n- Tests for each of these.\n\nThe hh-job-application-automation app works around this in `src/browser-session.mjs` (commit a868526 in konard/hh-job-application-automation).\n\n===== 180 Trace screenshots can leave a headful page stuck at its old size after a window resize\n## Problem\n\nA headful page that is being traced (`startTrace`, default `screenshots: 'checkpoints'`) can stop following its window size. After the user resizes the window, the page is still drawn at the old size in the top-left corner and the rest of the window stays blank. It stays that way until the page is reloaded.\n\nBy default, the browser must look and behave exactly like a real browser.\n\n## Cause\n\nThe trace recorder takes checkpoint screenshots with the engine's `page.screenshot({ type: 'png' })` (`src/traces/recorder.js`, `screenshot()`). For a viewport screenshot, Playwright 1.64 sends `Page.captureScreenshot` with a `clip` set to the current viewport. Chrome emulates the clip's size while it captures. If the window is resized during the capture, the emulated size can stay in place after the capture ends.\n\n## Reproduction\n\nMeasured with Chrome for Testing 156.0.8078.4 on macOS, Playwright 1.64, browser-commander 0.28 (0.32.1 has the same code):\n\n1. Start a headful Chrome and attach with `connectBrowser({ engine: 'playwright', cdpEndpoint })`.\n2. Keep taking screenshots in a loop while the window is resized in about 20 steps with `Browser.setWindowBounds`.\n3. Compare `innerWidth` with `outerWidth`.\n\n| Screenshot method | Drags where the page got stuck |\n|---|---|\n| `page.screenshot({ type: 'png' })` (Playwright) | 2 of 8 |\n| CDP `Page.captureScreenshot { format: 'png' }` (no clip) | 0 of 8 |\n| CDP `Page.captureScreenshot { fromSurface: false, captureBeyondViewport: false }` | 0 of 8 |\n| Trace checkpoints with the no-clip capture | 0 of 12 |\n\n## Suggested fix\n\nFor trace checkpoint screenshots, and any default capture of a page with no fixed viewport, use CDP `Page.captureScreenshot` without a `clip`. `captureStableViewport` already does this when `viewportSize()` is null.\n\nWorkaround in hh-job-application-automation: pass `startTrace` a `page` whose `screenshot` is the CDP capture without a clip.",

[2026-10-21T17:30:10.873Z] [INFO]         "content": "## Problem\n\nA browser started for automation must not take over the user's own browser or obstruct the view. In browser-commander 0.28.0, three things go wrong by default on macOS:\n\n1. **Chrome for Testing shows a bar over every page:** «Chrome for Testing v156.0.8078.4 is only for automated testing. For regular browsing, use a standard version of Chrome. [Download Chrome]». It takes vertical space in every window. `--disable-infobars` (the `no-infobars` restriction) does not remove it.\n2. **The user's Google Chrome is taken over:** `resolveLaunchExecutable()` prefers the installed Google Chrome (`channel: 'chrome'`). Started with another `--user-data-dir`, it is still the same app (`com.google.Chrome`) to macOS. When the user's own Chrome is not running, a click on Chrome in the Dock, ⌘T, or a link opened from another app goes to the automation window. An automation that keeps one tab then closes the user's tab.\n3. **The keychain is asked again and again:** Chrome for Testing started without `--use-mock-keychain` asks «Google Chrome for Testing wants to access key \"Chromium Safe Storage\" in your keychain» at each start.\n\n## Root cause and fix\n\n1. Chromium shows the Chrome for Testing bar unless `--test-type=gpu` is given. This is the only command-line value that skips it, from `chrome/browser/ui/startup/infobar_utils.cc`:\n   ```cpp\n   #if BUILDFLAG(CHROME_FOR_TESTING)\n   bool IsGpuTest() {\n     return base::CommandLine::ForCurrentProcess()->GetSwitchValueASCII(switches::kTestType) == \"gpu\";\n   }\n   #endif\n   ...\n   if (show_bad_flags_security_warnings) {\n   #if BUILDFLAG(CHROME_FOR_TESTING)\n     if (!IsGpuTest()) { ... ChromeForTestingInfoBarDelegate::Create(); }\n   #endif\n   ```\n   The only other way is the `CommandLineFlagSecurityWarningsEnabled` policy. `--test-type` also skips the later infobars (session crashed, default browser, …) and does not turn `navigator.webdriver` on.\n2. Launch Chrome for Testing (Playwright's or Puppeteer's), which is an app of its own (`com.google.chrome.for.testing`), and never the user's Google Chrome. The installed Google Chrome should be used only on request.\n3. Pass `--use-mock-keychain` to Chrome for Testing, so the keychain is never asked. Logins moved from a Google Chrome profile can be read by Google Chrome headless, which already has access to its own keychain entry, and then set with `Storage.setCookies`.\n\n## Requested\n\n- A default launch restriction `no-chrome-for-testing-infobar` (`--test-type=gpu`) whenever the executable is Chrome for Testing.\n- `resolveLaunchExecutable()` defaults to Chrome for Testing for automation, not to the user's Google Chrome.\n- `--use-mock-keychain` by default for Chrome for Testing.\n- Tests for each of these.\n\nThe hh-job-application-automation app works around this in `src/browser-session.mjs` (commit a868526 in konard/hh-job-application-automation).\n\npython/src/browser_commander/__init__.py:34:    CHROME_FOR_TESTING_RESTRICTIONS,\npython/src/browser_commander/__init__.py:261:    \"CHROME_FOR_TESTING_RESTRICTIONS\",\npython/src/browser_commander/browser/launch_executable.py:22:CHROME_FOR_TESTING_RESTRICTIONS: tuple[str, ...] = tuple(\npython/src/browser_commander/browser/launch_executable.py:31:_CHROME_FOR_TESTING_DIRECTORIES = frozenset(\npython/src/browser_commander/browser/launch_executable.py:45:def is_chrome_for_testing(executable_path: Any) -> bool:\npython/src/browser_commander/browser/launch_executable.py:56:        \"chrome for testing\" in segment or segment in _CHROME_FOR_TESTING_DIRECTORIES\npython/src/browser_commander/browser/launch_executable.py:72:def default_restrictions_for(\npython/src/browser_commander/browser/launch_executable.py:85:        return list(CHROME_FOR_TESTING_RESTRICTIONS)",

The whole command line is\n`--user-data-dir=<fresh temporary profile> --remote-debugging-port=<reserved port> about:blank`:\nno automation switches, so `navigator.webdriver` is `false`, there is no\n\"controlled by automated test software\" or unsupported-flag infobar, and\nextensions, sync, translation and every other browser feature behave as in a\nhand-started Chrome. The temporary profile is deleted by `browser.close()`.\n\n```javascript\nconst { browser, page } = await launchBrowser({\n  engine: 'playwright',\n  channel: 'msedge', // or executablePath: '/usr/bin/google-chrome'\n  userDataDir: '/tmp/my-profile', // keep the profile instead of a temporary one\n  extraArgs: ['--lang=en-US'],\n  // Opt-in restrictions, by name (see the table linked below).\n  restrictions: ['no-sync', 'no-translate'],\n});\n```\n\nEvery switch Browser Commander used to add on its own is available as a named\n[launch restriction](https://github.com/link-foundation/browser-commander/blob/main/docs/feature-parity.md#launch-command-line-and-opt-in-restrictions);\n`restrictions: ['legacy-defaults']` restores the old `CHROME_ARGS`. Pass\n`launch: 'engine'` to use Playwright's `launchPersistentContext()` or\n`puppeteer.launch()` instead; the engine then adds its own switches, and\n`ignoreDefaultArgs` removes them.\n\nAttach to a Chrome-family browser that is already listening for CDP connections:\n\n```javascript\nimport { connectBrowser, makeBrowserCommander } from 'browser-commander';\n\nconst { browser, page } = await connectBrowser({\n  engine: 'playwright', // or 'puppeteer'\n  cdpEndpoint: 'http://127.0.0.1:9222',\n});\nconst commander = makeBrowserCommander({ page });\n```\n\nAttachment cannot change the existing process's launch arguments. Start it\nwith a fixed `--remote-debugging-port` and a dedicated `--user-data-dir`, or\nlet `launchBrowser()`/`launchRealBrowser()` start it.\n\n`launchRealBrowser()` is the lower-level helper behind the default launch: it\nfinds and starts an installed Chrome, Edge, Brave, or Chromium on a reserved\nloopback port, confirms from the browser's own `DevTools listening on` line\nthat the port is really its own (retrying on a port race), and attaches. It\nalways uses a dedicated profile; Chrome 136 and newer do not honor remote\ndebugging switches for the default profile. See the\n[Chrome remote-debugging security change](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/remote-debugging-port).\n\n```javascript\nimport { launchRealBrowser } from 'browser-commander';\n\nconst connection = await launchRealBrowser({\n  engine: 'puppeteer',\n  channel: 'chrome',\n  userDataDir: '/tmp/my-automation-profile',\n  extraArgs: ['--lang=en-US'],\n  restrictions: ['no-default-browser-check'],\n----\n```\n\nFor trace budgets/privacy, persistent session adoption and heartbeats, CDP\n`noDefaults`, overlay reporting, and the `readyOn`/`concurrency` trigger migration,\nsee [trace and session hardening](https://github.com/link-foundation/browser-commander/blob/f5e426d6933c681189c4989bac182a1558d8edb8/docs/trace-session-hardening.md).\n\n## API Reference\n\n### launchBrowser(options)\n\n```javascript\nconst { browser, page, close } = await launchBrowser({\n  engine: 'playwright', // 'playwright' or 'puppeteer'\n  launch: 'real', // 'real' (start the installed browser, attach) or 'engine'\n  channel: 'chrome', // or executablePath; defaults to the installed Chrome\n  headless: false, // Run in headless mode\n  userDataDir: undefined, // Keep a profile; default is a fresh temporary one\n  restrictions: [], // Opt-in restrictions such as 'no-extensions', 'no-sync'\n  slowMo: 0, // Slow down operations (ms)\n  verbose: false, // Enable debug logging\n  args: ['--no-sandbox'], // Custom Chrome args to append\n  storageState: './session-state.json', // Saved cookies and localStorage, as a path or object\n  interruption: 'managed', // 'caller' leaves Ctrl+C (SIGINT) to your own handler\n});\n```\n\nWith Playwright, `browser` is the attached browser's default context, so\n`browser.pages()`, `browser.newPage()` and `browser.close()` work as they did\nwith the persistent context. `close()` (and `browser.close()`) closes the\nbrowser and deletes a temporary profile. The result also carries `launch`,\n`userDataDir`, `temporaryProfile` and the exact `args` the browser was started\nwith.\n\nThe `args` option allows passing custom Chrome arguments, which is useful for headless server environments (Docker, CI/CD) that require flags like `--no-sandbox`.\n\nThe `storageState` option accepts a Playwright-compatible JSON path or object.\nEach engine restores its cookies and origin-specific localStorage before\nnavigation, including when Playwright uses a persistent context.\n\n### connectBrowser(options)\n\nConnect to an existing Chrome-family browser over an HTTP or WebSocket CDP\nendpoint. Exactly one of `cdpEndpoint` and `wsEndpoint` is required. The raw\n`browser` and `page` work with both the underlying engine API and\n`makeBrowserCommander({ page })`.\n\n```javascript\nconst { browser, page } = await connectBrowser({\n  engine: 'playwright',\n  wsEndpoint: 'ws://127.0.0.1:9222/devtools/browser/<id>',\n  timeout: 30_000,\n  seedCookies: [\n    { name: 'session', value: 'saved', url: 'https://example.com' },\n  ],\n});\n```\n\nPlaywright accepts `timeout` and Puppeteer accepts `protocolTimeout`.\n`storageState` can also seed Playwright-compatible cookies and localStorage.\n\n### launchRealBrowser(options)\n\nStart an installed browser and connect through `connectBrowser()`. Use\n`channel` (`chrome`, `chrome-beta`, `chrome-dev`, `chrome-canary`, `msedge`,\n`msedge-beta`, `msedge-dev`, `msedge-canary`, `brave`, or `chromium`) or an\nexplicit `executablePath`. Without `userDataDir` it creates a fresh temporary\nprofile that `close()` deletes; it rejects known default browser-profile paths,\nprotects its remote-debugging switches, reserves a loopback port (or uses\n`remoteDebuggingPort`, never `0`), and returns the spawned `browserProcess`,\n`cdpEndpoint`, `remoteDebuggingPort`, `executablePath`, `userDataDir`,\n`temporaryProfile` and `args` alongside `{ browser, page, close }`.\n`launchAndConnectRealBrowser()` is an alias with identical behavior.\n`restrictions` opts into named restrictions, `args`/`extraArgs` append custom\nswitches, and `env` adds environment variables for the browser process only.\n\nThe launch is clean by default, so signing in with a Google account works\n(a nonexistent address shows \"Couldn't find your Google Account\" rather than\n\"This browser or app may not be secure\"). Pass `migrateFrom` to opt into a\nread-only migration from an installed browser's main profile before the launch;\nthe migrated cookies are seeded automatically and the returned session carries a\n`migration` report (see `migrateProfile()` below):\n----\n`selenium-webdriver` (an optional peer dependency). `launchWebDriver()` finds a\ndriver (`driverPath`, then `PATH`, then the Selenium Manager bundled with\n`selenium-webdriver`, which downloads a chromedriver/geckodriver matching the\nbrowser), starts it on a reserved loopback port, waits for `/status`, and opens\na session with a fresh temporary profile that `close()` deletes:\n\n```javascript\nimport { launchWebDriver, makeBrowserCommander } from 'browser-commander';\n\nconst { driver, page, close } = await launchWebDriver({\n  browser: 'chrome', // or 'firefox'\n  headless: false,\n  bidi: true, // WebDriver BiDi: console/dialog/network events, preload scripts\n  // executablePath, driverPath, userDataDir, args, restrictions, env\n});\nconst commander = makeBrowserCommander({ page }); // commander.engine === 'selenium'\n\npage.on('console', (message) => console.log(message.text())); // needs bidi\nawait commander.goto({ url: 'https://example.com' });\nawait commander.fill({ selector: 'input[name=\"q\"]', text: 'hello' });\nawait commander.click({ selector: 'button[type=\"submit\"]' });\nconst pdf = await page.pdf({ format: 'A4' }); // W3C Print Page\nawait close();\n```\n\n`page` is a `WebDriverPage`: a Puppeteer-shaped facade over the `driver`\n(`evaluate`, `$`, `$$`, `keyboard`, `mouse`, `screenshot`, `pdf`, `cookies`,\n`on`), so the rest of Browser Commander runs unchanged. `makeBrowserCommander()`\nalso accepts a bare selenium `WebDriver` and wraps it. On the adapter\n(`createEngineAdapter(page, 'selenium')`), `onConsoleMessage(handler)`,\n`onNavigation(handler)`, `onBidiEvent(method, handler)` and\n`navigate(url, {wait})` expose BiDi `log.entryAdded` and `browsingContext`\ndirectly; they throw when the session has no BiDi.\n\nChrome gets the same command line as `launchRealBrowser()`\n(`--user-data-dir` and a fixed `--remote-debugging-port`), and every switch\nchromedriver would add on its own - `--enable-automation`,\n`--remote-debugging-port=0`, `--password-store=[REDACTED] `--test-type=webdriver`\nand 16 more - is excluded, so `navigator.webdriver` is `false` headful and\nheadless. `connectWebDriver({ serverUrl, capabilities })` opens a session on a\nserver that is already running (a Selenium Grid, a cloud provider); pass\n`capabilities: { webSocketUrl: true }` for BiDi. Media emulation, fingerprint\noverrides and managed downloads need CDP and throw on this engine; see\n[docs/feature-parity.md](https://github.com/link-foundation/browser-commander/blob/main/docs/feature-parity.md#webdriver-engine).\n\n### listBrowserProfiles(options)\n\nDiscover profiles for the browsers in the shared catalogue, including Safari.\nPass an optional `browser` to narrow discovery. Each result contains\n`{ browser, name, displayName, path, isDefault }`. If Safari's profile catalogue\ncannot be read, a `Profiles` entry carries `error` alongside readable profiles.\n\n### migrateProfile(options)\n\nCopy data from an installed browser's main profile into a dedicated target\nprofile directory (usually the `Default` folder of a `launchRealBrowser()`\n`userDataDir`). This is the same migration `launchRealBrowser({ migrateFrom })`\nruns, exposed directly. It is **opt-in and strictly read-only** on the source:\nSQLite databases (`History`, `Top Sites`, cookies, Firefox `places.sqlite`) are\ncopied through the SQLite Online Backup API so a running browser is never\ndisturbed, and JSON files (`Bookmarks`, `Preferences`) are copied as is.\n\n```javascript\nimport { migrateProfile } from 'browser-commander';\n\nconst report = await migrateProfile({\n  from: { browser: 'chrome', profile: 'Default' },\n  to: '/path/to/dedicated/User Data/Default',\n  targetBrowser: 'chrome', // launching channel, for key derivation\n  include: [\n    'cookies',\n    'bookmarks',\n    'history',\n    'passwords',\n    'preferences',\n    'extensions',\n  ],\n  domains: ['github.com'], // optional cookies/history/passwords filter\n});\n```\n\nThe report is `{ source, target, migrated, skipped, warnings, cookies }`:\n`migrated` counts each data class, `cookies` holds the seedable Playwright-shape\ncookies, and `skipped`/`warnings` explain everything that could not be migrated\nverbatim, for example:\n\n- **DBSC-bound Google cookies** (`__Secure-1PSIDTS`/`3PSIDTS`/`SIDTS`) are\n  reported `dbsc-bound`: their Device Bound Session Credentials key cannot leave\n  the source profile, so those sessions expire quickly and are not copied.\n- **Windows app-bound `v20`** passwords/cookies are reported `app-bound-v20`\n  because they require the browser's privileged elevation service.\n- **Migrated extensions** are reported `mac-will-not-validate`: Chromium's\n  `Secure Preferences` MAC cannot be forged externally, so migrated extensions",

Start it\nwith a fixed `--remote-debugging-port` and a dedicated `--user-data-dir`, or\nlet `launchBrowser()`/`launchRealBrowser()` start it.\n\n`launchRealBrowser()` is the lower-level helper behind the default launch: it\nfinds and starts an installed Chrome, Edge, Brave, or Chromium on a reserved\nloopback port, confirms from the browser's own `DevTools listening on` line\nthat the port is really its own (retrying on a port race), and attaches. It\nalways uses a dedicated profile; Chrome 136 and newer do not honor remote\ndebugging switches for the default profile. See the\n[Chrome remote-debugging security change](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/remote-debugging-port).\n\n```javascript\nimport { launchRealBrowser } from 'browser-commander';\n\nconst connection = await launchRealBrowser({\n  engine: 'puppeteer',\n  channel: 'chrome',\n  userDataDir: '/tmp/my-automation-profile',\n  extraArgs: ['--lang=en-US'],\n  restrictions: ['no-default-browser-check'],\n----\n```\n\nFor trace budgets/privacy, persistent session adoption and heartbeats, CDP\n`noDefaults`, overlay reporting, and the `readyOn`/`concurrency` trigger migration,\nsee [trace and session hardening](https://github.com/link-foundation/browser-commander/blob/f5e426d6933c681189c4989bac182a1558d8edb8/docs/trace-session-hardening.md).\n\n## API Reference\n\n### launchBrowser(options)\n\n```javascript\nconst { browser, page, close } = await launchBrowser({\n  engine: 'playwright', // 'playwright' or 'puppeteer'\n  launch: 'real', // 'real' (start the installed browser, attach) or 'engine'\n  channel: 'chrome', // or executablePath; defaults to the installed Chrome\n  headless: false, // Run in headless mode\n  userDataDir: undefined, // Keep a profile; default is a fresh temporary one\n  restrictions: [], // Opt-in restrictions such as 'no-extensions', 'no-sync'\n  slowMo: 0, // Slow down operations (ms)\n  verbose: false, // Enable debug logging\n  args: ['--no-sandbox'], // Custom Chrome args to append\n  storageState: './session-state.json', // Saved cookies and localStorage, as a path or object\n  interruption: 'managed', // 'caller' leaves Ctrl+C (SIGINT) to your own handler\n});\n```\n\nWith Playwright, `browser` is the attached browser's default context, so\n`browser.pages()`, `browser.newPage()` and `browser.close()` work as they did\nwith the persistent context. `close()` (and `browser.close()`) closes the\nbrowser and deletes a temporary profile. The result also carries `launch`,\n`userDataDir`, `temporaryProfile` and the exact `args` the browser was started\nwith.\n\nThe `args` option allows passing custom Chrome arguments, which is useful for headless server environments (Docker, CI/CD) that require flags like `--no-sandbox`.\n\nThe `storageState` option accepts a Playwright-compatible JSON path or object.\nEach engine restores its cookies and origin-specific localStorage before\nnavigation, including when Playwright uses a persistent context.\n\n### connectBrowser(options)\n\nConnect to an existing Chrome-family browser over an HTTP or WebSocket CDP\nendpoint. Exactly one of `cdpEndpoint` and `wsEndpoint` is required. The raw\n`browser` and `page` work with both the underlying engine API and\n`makeBrowserCommander({ page })`.\n\n```javascript\nconst { browser, page } = await connectBrowser({\n  engine: 'playwright',\n  wsEndpoint: 'ws://127.0.0.1:9222/devtools/browser/<id>',\n  timeout: 30_000,\n  seedCookies: [\n    { name: 'session', value: 'saved', url: 'https://example.com' },\n  ],\n});\n```\n\nPlaywright accepts `timeout` and Puppeteer accepts `protocolTimeout`.\n`storageState` can also seed Playwright-compatible cookies and localStorage.\n\n### launchRealBrowser(options)\n\nStart an installed browser and connect through `connectBrowser()`. Use\n`channel` (`chrome`, `chrome-beta`, `chrome-dev`, `chrome-canary`, `msedge`,\n`msedge-beta`, `msedge-dev`, `msedge-canary`, `brave`, or `chromium`) or an\nexplicit `executablePath`. Without `userDataDir` it creates a fresh temporary\nprofile that `close()` deletes; it rejects known default browser-profile paths,\nprotects its remote-debugging switches, reserves a loopback port (or uses\n`remoteDebuggingPort`, never `0`), and returns the spawned `browserProcess`,\n`cdpEndpoint`, `remoteDebuggingPort`, `executablePath`, `userDataDir`,\n`temporaryProfile` and `args` alongside `{ browser, page, close }`.\n`launchAndConnectRealBrowser()` is an alias with identical behavior.\n`restrictions` opts into named restrictions, `args`/`extraArgs` append custom\nswitches, and `env` adds environment variables for the browser process only.\n\nThe launch is clean by default, so signing in with a Google account works\n(a nonexistent address shows \"Couldn't find your Google Account\" rather than\n\"This browser or app may not be secure\"). Pass `migrateFrom` to opt into a\nread-only migration from an installed browser's main profile before the launch;\nthe migrated cookies are seeded automatically and the returned session carries a\n`migration` report (see `migrateProfile()` below):\n----\n`selenium-webdriver` (an optional peer dependency). `launchWebDriver()` finds a\ndriver (`driverPath`, then `PATH`, then the Selenium Manager bundled with\n`selenium-webdriver`, which downloads a chromedriver/geckodriver matching the\nbrowser), starts it on a reserved loopback port, waits for `/status`, and opens\na session with a fresh temporary profile that `close()` deletes:\n\n```javascript\nimport { launchWebDriver, makeBrowserCommander } from 'browser-commander';\n\nconst { driver, page, close } = await launchWebDriver({\n  browser: 'chrome', // or 'firefox'\n  headless: false,\n  bidi: true, // WebDriver BiDi: console/dialog/network events, preload scripts\n  // executablePath, driverPath, userDataDir, args, restrictions, env\n});\nconst commander = makeBrowserCommander({ page }); // commander.engine === 'selenium'\n\npage.on('console', (message) => console.log(message.text())); // needs bidi\nawait commander.goto({ url: 'https://example.com' });\nawait commander.fill({ selector: 'input[name=\"q\"]', text: 'hello' });\nawait commander.click({ selector: 'button[type=\"submit\"]' });\nconst pdf = await page.pdf({ format: 'A4' }); // W3C Print Page\nawait close();\n```\n\n`page` is a `WebDriverPage`: a Puppeteer-shaped facade over the `driver`\n(`evaluate`, `$`, `$$`, `keyboard`, `mouse`, `screenshot`, `pdf`, `cookies`,\n`on`), so the rest of Browser Commander runs unchanged. `makeBrowserCommander()`\nalso accepts a bare selenium `WebDriver` and wraps it. On the adapter\n(`createEngineAdapter(page, 'selenium')`), `onConsoleMessage(handler)`,\n`onNavigation(handler)`, `onBidiEvent(method, handler)` and\n`navigate(url, {wait})` expose BiDi `log.entryAdded` and `browsingContext`\ndirectly; they throw when the session has no BiDi.\n\nChrome gets the same command line as `launchRealBrowser()`\n(`--user-data-dir` and a fixed `--remote-debugging-port`), and every switch\nchromedriver would add on its own - `--enable-automation`,\n`--remote-debugging-port=0`, `--password-store=[REDACTED] `--test-type=webdriver`\nand 16 more - is excluded, so `navigator.webdriver` is `false` headful and\nheadless. `connectWebDriver({ serverUrl, capabilities })` opens a session on a\nserver that is already running (a Selenium Grid, a cloud provider); pass\n`capabilities: { webSocketUrl: true }` for BiDi. Media emulation, fingerprint\noverrides and managed downloads need CDP and throw on this engine; see\n[docs/feature-parity.md](https://github.com/link-foundation/browser-commander/blob/main/docs/feature-parity.md#webdriver-engine).\n\n### listBrowserProfiles(options)\n\nDiscover profiles for the browsers in the shared catalogue, including Safari.\nPass an optional `browser` to narrow discovery. Each result contains\n`{ browser, name, displayName, path, isDefault }`. If Safari's profile catalogue\ncannot be read, a `Profiles` entry carries `error` alongside readable profiles.\n\n### migrateProfile(options)\n\nCopy data from an installed browser's main profile into a dedicated target\nprofile directory (usually the `Default` folder of a `launchRealBrowser()`\n`userDataDir`). This is the same migration `launchRealBrowser({ migrateFrom })`\nruns, exposed directly. It is **opt-in and strictly read-only** on the source:\nSQLite databases (`History`, `Top Sites`, cookies, Firefox `places.sqlite`) are\ncopied through the SQLite Online Backup API so a running browser is never\ndisturbed, and JSON files (`Bookmarks`, `Preferences`) are copied as is.\n\n```javascript\nimport { migrateProfile } from 'browser-commander';\n\nconst report = await migrateProfile({\n  from: { browser: 'chrome', profile: 'Default' },\n  to: '/path/to/dedicated/User Data/Default',\n  targetBrowser: 'chrome', // launching channel, for key derivation\n  include: [\n    'cookies',\n    'bookmarks',\n    'history',\n    'passwords',\n    'preferences',\n    'extensions',\n  ],\n  domains: ['github.com'], // optional cookies/history/passwords filter\n});\n```\n\nThe report is `{ source, target, migrated, skipped, warnings, cookies }`:\n`migrated` counts each data class, `cookies` holds the seedable Playwright-shape\ncookies, and `skipped`/`warnings` explain everything that could not be migrated\nverbatim, for example:\n\n- **DBSC-bound Google cookies** (`__Secure-1PSIDTS`/`3PSIDTS`/`SIDTS`) are\n  reported `dbsc-bound`: their Device Bound Session Credentials key cannot leave\n  the source profile, so those sessions expire quickly and are not copied.\n- **Windows app-bound `v20`** passwords/cookies are reported `app-bound-v20`\n  because they require the browser's privileged elevation service.\n- **Migrated extensions** are reported `mac-will-not-validate`: Chromium's\n  `Secure Preferences` MAC cannot be forged externally, so migrated extensions",

[2026-10-21T18:01:45.276Z] [INFO]           "content": "# Chrome for Testing by default\n\nWithout a `channel` or an `executablePath` (`executable_path` in Python and\nRust), every engine starts **Chrome for Testing**: the browser\n`npx playwright install chromium`, `npx puppeteer browsers install chrome`,\n`python -m playwright install chromium` or Selenium Manager downloads. It is\nnever the user's own Google Chrome, so automation does not share an\napplication, a Dock icon or a keychain entry with the browser the person uses\n(issue #179). The installed Google Chrome is started only on request:\n\n| Language   | Chrome for Testing (default) | The installed Google Chrome                         |\n| ---------- | ---------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |\n| JavaScript | `launchBrowser({ engine })`  | `launchBrowser({ engine, channel: 'chrome' })`      |\n| Python     | `launch_browser(engine=...)` | `launch_browser(engine=..., channel=\"chrome\")`      |\n| Rust       | `LaunchOptions::playwright()` | `LaunchOptions::playwright().channel(\"chrome\")`    |\n\n## Which download each engine uses\n\n| Engine                  | Chrome for Testing it starts                                                                 |\n| ----------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |\n| Playwright (JS, Python) | Playwright's `chromium.executablePath()` / `chromium.executable_path`.                        |\n| Puppeteer (JS)          | Puppeteer's `executablePath()`.                                                               |\n| Selenium (JS)           | Playwright's, then Puppeteer's.                                                               |\n| Selenium (Python)       | Playwright's; `launch: 'engine'` lets Selenium Manager download one.                          |\n| Rust engines            | The one Playwright or Puppeteer reports through Node, else the newest in the download caches. |\n\nWhen none is installed the launch fails with the command that installs it, or\nsays to pass `channel: 'chrome'`; it never falls back to Google Chrome\nsilently.\n\nSelenium attaches through a ChromeDriver, and ChromeDriver drives only the\nChrome release it was built for. The driver is resolved for the Chrome for\nTesting that was started, through Selenium Manager's `--browser-path`; a\n`chromedriver` on `PATH`, which belongs to the installed Google Chrome, is\nnot used for Chrome for Testing.\n\n## Default restrictions: no infobar, no keychain prompt\n\nChrome for Testing shows a \"Chrome for Testing is only for automated testing\"\nbar under the toolbar, and on macOS it asks for the keychain password the first\ntime it encrypts cookies or passwords. A launch of Chrome for Testing therefore\nadds the `chrome-for-testing` preset of\n[launch restrictions](feature-parity.md#launch-command-line-and-opt-in-restrictions):\n\n| Restriction                     | Switch                | Effect                                                                                                                                         |\n| ------------------------------- | --------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |\n| `no-chrome-for-testing-infobar` | `--test-type=gpu`     | Hides the bar. Chromium skips it only for this test type, which also skips the unsupported-flag and other startup infobars, and nothing else. |\n| `mock-keychain`                 | `--use-mock-keychain` | Encrypts with a fixed key instead of a \"Chromium Safe Storage\" keychain entry, so macOS never prompts.                                         |\n\nAny other browser - Google Chrome, Edge, Brave, Chromium - gets no default\nrestriction: its command line stays the one a person would type. The session\nreports what was added as `defaultRestrictions` (`default_restrictions` in\nPython and Rust), and `measureParity()` counts these switches as requested.\n\n`defaultRestrictions: []` opts out, and any other list replaces the preset:\n\n```js\nawait launchBrowser({ engine: 'playwright', defaultRestrictions: [] });\n```\n\n```python\nawait launch_browser(engine=\"playwright\", default_restrictions=[])\n```\n\n```rust\nlaunch_browser(LaunchOptions::playwright().default_restrictions(Vec::<String>::new())).await?;\n```\n\n`isChromeForTesting(path)` / `is_chrome_for_testing(path)` and\n`defaultRestrictionsFor(path, requested)` / `default_restrictions_for(path,\nrequested)` expose the same decision. A path is Chrome for Testing when it is\ninside a `chrome-linux64`, `chrome-win64`, `chrome-win32`, `chrome-mac-x64` or\n`chrome-mac-arm64` directory, inside Selenium Manager's\n`selenium/chrome/<platform>/<version>` cache, or names a\n`Google Chrome for Testing` application.\n\n## Profile migration\n\n`migrateFrom` encrypts passwords and cookies with the key of the browser that\nstarts. With the default `mock-keychain` that is Chromium's fixed mock key;\nwithout it, Chrome for Testing uses its own \"Chromium Safe Storage\" keychain\nitem rather than Google Chrome's \"Chrome Safe Storage\".\n\n## Verifying it\n\n`js/tests/e2e/chrome-for-testing.e2e.test.js` launches each JavaScript engine\nheadfully, reads `chrome://version` to check the executable and both switches,\nand measures that the opt-out window is taller by the infobar. The\n`Browser Parity` workflow installs every engine's Chrome for Testing and runs\nit, alongside the Python and Rust default launches.\n"

[2026-10-21T18:01:45.356Z] [INFO]     "content": "# Chrome for Testing by default\n\nWithout a `channel` or an `executablePath` (`executable_path` in Python and\nRust), every engine starts **Chrome for Testing**: the browser\n`npx playwright install chromium`, `npx puppeteer browsers install chrome`,\n`python -m playwright install chromium` or Selenium Manager downloads. It is\nnever the user's own Google Chrome, so automation does not share an\napplication, a Dock icon or a keychain entry with the browser the person uses\n(issue #179). The installed Google Chrome is started only on request:\n\n| Language   | Chrome for Testing (default) | The installed Google Chrome                         |\n| ---------- | ---------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |\n| JavaScript | `launchBrowser({ engine })`  | `launchBrowser({ engine, channel: 'chrome' })`      |\n| Python     | `launch_browser(engine=...)` | `launch_browser(engine=..., channel=\"chrome\")`      |\n| Rust       | `LaunchOptions::playwright()` | `LaunchOptions::playwright().channel(\"chrome\")`    |\n\n## Which download each engine uses\n\n| Engine                  | Chrome for Testing it starts                                                                 |\n| ----------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |\n| Playwright (JS, Python) | Playwright's `chromium.executablePath()` / `chromium.executable_path`.                        |\n| Puppeteer (JS)          | Puppeteer's `executablePath()`.                                                               |\n| Selenium (JS)           | Playwright's, then Puppeteer's.                                                               |\n| Selenium (Python)       | Playwright's; `launch: 'engine'` lets Selenium Manager download one.                          |\n| Rust engines            | The one Playwright or Puppeteer reports through Node, else the newest in the download caches. |\n\nWhen none is installed the launch fails with the command that installs it, or\nsays to pass `channel: 'chrome'`; it never falls back to Google Chrome\nsilently.\n\nSelenium attaches through a ChromeDriver, and ChromeDriver drives only the\nChrome release it was built for. The driver is resolved for the Chrome for\nTesting that was started, through Selenium Manager's `--browser-path`; a\n`chromedriver` on `PATH`, which belongs to the installed Google Chrome, is\nnot used for Chrome for Testing.\n\n## Default restrictions: no infobar, no keychain prompt\n\nChrome for Testing shows a \"Chrome for Testing is only for automated testing\"\nbar under the toolbar, and on macOS it asks for the keychain password the first\ntime it encrypts cookies or passwords. A launch of Chrome for Testing therefore\nadds the `chrome-for-testing` preset of\n[launch restrictions](feature-parity.md#launch-command-line-and-opt-in-restrictions):\n\n| Restriction                     | Switch                | Effect                                                                                                                                         |\n| ------------------------------- | --------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |\n| `no-chrome-for-testing-infobar` | `--test-type=gpu`     | Hides the bar. Chromium skips it only for this test type, which also skips the unsupported-flag and other startup infobars, and nothing else. |\n| `mock-keychain`                 | `--use-mock-keychain` | Encrypts with a fixed key instead of a \"Chromium Safe Storage\" keychain entry, so macOS never prompts.                                         |\n\nAny other browser - Google Chrome, Edge, Brave, Chromium - gets no default\nrestriction: its command line stays the one a person would type. The session\nreports what was added as `defaultRestrictions` (`default_restrictions` in\nPython and Rust), and `measureParity()` counts these switches as requested.\n\n`defaultRestrictions: []` opts out, and any other list replaces the preset:\n\n```js\nawait launchBrowser({ engine: 'playwright', defaultRestrictions: [] });\n```\n\n```python\nawait launch_browser(engine=\"playwright\", default_restrictions=[])\n```\n\n```rust\nlaunch_browser(LaunchOptions::playwright().default_restrictions(Vec::<String>::new())).await?;\n```\n\n`isChromeForTesting(path)` / `is_chrome_for_testing(path)` and\n`defaultRestrictionsFor(path, requested)` / `default_restrictions_for(path,\nrequested)` expose the same decision. A path is Chrome for Testing when it is\ninside a `chrome-linux64`, `chrome-win64`, `chrome-win32`, `chrome-mac-x64` or\n`chrome-mac-arm64` directory, inside Selenium Manager's\n`selenium/chrome/<platform>/<version>` cache, or names a\n`Google Chrome for Testing` application.\n\n## Profile migration\n\n`migrateFrom` encrypts passwords and cookies with the key of the browser that\nstarts. With the default `mock-keychain` that is Chromium's fixed mock key;\nwithout it, Chrome for Testing uses its own \"Chromium Safe Storage\" keychain\nitem rather than Google Chrome's \"Chrome Safe Storage\".\n\n## Verifying it\n\n`js/tests/e2e/chrome-for-testing.e2e.test.js` launches each JavaScript engine\nheadfully, reads `chrome://version` to check the executable and both switches,\nand measures that the opt-out window is taller by the infobar. The\n`Browser Parity` workflow installs every engine's Chrome for Testing and runs\nit, alongside the Python and Rust default launches.\n",

[2026-10-21T18:17:46.044Z] [INFO]     "originalFile": "# Chrome for Testing by default\n\nWithout a `channel` or an `executablePath` (`executable_path` in Python and\nRust), every engine starts **Chrome for Testing**: the browser\n`npx playwright install chromium`, `npx puppeteer browsers install chrome`,\n`python -m playwright install chromium` or Selenium Manager downloads. It is\nnever the user's own Google Chrome, so automation does not share an\napplication, a Dock icon or a keychain entry with the browser the person uses\n(issue #179). The installed Google Chrome is started only on request:\n\n| Language   | Chrome for Testing (default)  | The installed Google Chrome                     |\n| ---------- | ----------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |\n| JavaScript | `launchBrowser({ engine })`   | `launchBrowser({ engine, channel: 'chrome' })`  |\n| Python     | `launch_browser(engine=...)`  | `launch_browser(engine=..., channel=\"chrome\")`  |\n| Rust       | `LaunchOptions::playwright()` | `LaunchOptions::playwright().channel(\"chrome\")` |\n\n## Which download each engine uses\n\n| Engine                  | Chrome for Testing it starts                                                                  |\n| ----------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |\n| Playwright (JS, Python) | Playwright's `chromium.executablePath()` / `chromium.executable_path`.                        |\n| Puppeteer (JS)          | Puppeteer's `executablePath()`.                                                               |\n| Selenium (JS)           | Playwright's, then Puppeteer's.                                                               |\n| Selenium (Python)       | Playwright's, else the one Selenium Manager downloads.                                        |\n| Rust engines            | The one Playwright or Puppeteer reports through Node, else the newest in the download caches. |\n\nWhen no engine has one, the launch fails with the command that installs it, or\nsays to pass `channel: 'chrome'`; it never falls back to Google Chrome\nsilently.\n\nSelenium attaches through a ChromeDriver, and ChromeDriver drives only the\nChrome release it was built for. The driver is resolved for the Chrome for\nTesting that was started, through Selenium Manager's `--browser-path`; a\n`chromedriver` on `PATH`, which belongs to the installed Google Chrome, is\nnot used for Chrome for Testing.\n\n## Default restrictions: no infobar, no keychain prompt\n\nChrome for Testing shows a \"Chrome for Testing is only for automated testing\"\nbar under the toolbar, and on macOS it asks for the keychain password the first\ntime it encrypts cookies or passwords. A launch of Chrome for Testing therefore\nadds the `chrome-for-testing` preset of\n[launch restrictions](feature-parity.md#launch-command-line-and-opt-in-restrictions):\n\n| Restriction                     | Switch                | Effect                                                                                                                                        |\n| ------------------------------- | --------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |\n| `no-chrome-for-testing-infobar` | `--test-type=gpu`     | Hides the bar. Chromium skips it only for this test type, which also skips the unsupported-flag and other startup infobars, and nothing else. |\n| `mock-keychain`                 | `--use-mock-keychain` | Encrypts with a fixed key instead of a \"Chromium Safe Storage\" keychain entry, so macOS never prompts.                                        |\n\nAny other browser - Google Chrome, Edge, Brave, Chromium - gets no default\nrestriction: its command line stays the one a person would type. The session\nreports what was added as `defaultRestrictions` (`default_restrictions` in\nPython and Rust), and `measureParity()` counts these switches as requested.\n\n`defaultRestrictions: []` opts out, and any other list replaces the preset:\n\n```js\nawait launchBrowser({ engine: 'playwright', defaultRestrictions: [] });\n```\n\n```python\nawait launch_browser(engine=\"playwright\", default_restrictions=[])\n```\n\n```rust\nlaunch_browser(LaunchOptions::playwright().default_restrictions(Vec::<String>::new())).await?;\n```\n\n`isChromeForTesting(path)` / `is_chrome_for_testing(path)` and\n`defaultRestrictionsFor(path, requested)` / `default_restrictions_for(path,\nrequested)` expose the same decision. A path is Chrome for Testing when it is\ninside a `chrome-linux64`, `chrome-win64`, `chrome-win32`, `chrome-mac-x64` or\n`chrome-mac-arm64` directory, inside Selenium Manager's\n`selenium/chrome/<platform>/<version>` cache, or names a\n`Google Chrome for Testing` application.\n\n## Profile migration\n\n`migrateFrom` encrypts passwords and cookies with the key of the browser that\nstarts. With the default `mock-keychain` that is Chromium's fixed mock key;\nwithout it, Chrome for Testing uses its own \"Chromium Safe Storage\" keychain\nitem rather than Google Chrome's \"Chrome Safe Storage\".\n\n## Verifying it\n\n`js/tests/e2e/chrome-for-testing.e2e.test.js` launches each JavaScript engine\nheadfully, reads `chrome://version` to check the executable and both switches,\nand measures that the opt-out window is taller by the infobar. The\n`Browser Parity` workflow installs every engine's Chrome for Testing and runs\nit, alongside the Python and Rust default launches.\n",

After the user resizes the window, the page is still drawn at the old size in the top-left corner and the rest of the window stays blank. It stays that way until the page is reloaded.\n\nBy default, the browser must look and behave exactly like a real browser.\n\n## Cause\n\nThe trace recorder takes checkpoint screenshots with the engine's `page.screenshot({ type: 'png' })` (`src/traces/recorder.js`, `screenshot()`). For a viewport screenshot, Playwright 1.64 sends `Page.captureScreenshot` with a `clip` set to the current viewport. Chrome emulates the clip's size while it captures. If the window is resized during the capture, the emulated size can stay in place after the capture ends.\n\n## Reproduction\n\nMeasured with Chrome for Testing 156.0.8078.4 on macOS, Playwright 1.64, browser-commander 0.28 (0.32.1 has the same code):\n\n1. Start a headful Chrome and attach with `connectBrowser({ engine: 'playwright', cdpEndpoint })`.\n2. Keep taking screenshots in a loop while the window is resized in about 20 steps with `Browser.setWindowBounds`.\n3. Compare `innerWidth` with `outerWidth`.\n\n| Screenshot method | Drags where the page got stuck |\n|---|---|\n| `page.screenshot({ type: 'png' })` (Playwright) | 2 of 8 |\n| CDP `Page.captureScreenshot { format: 'png' }` (no clip) | 0 of 8 |\n| CDP `Page.captureScreenshot { fromSurface: false, captureBeyondViewport: false }` | 0 of 8 |\n| Trace checkpoints with the no-clip capture | 0 of 12 |\n\n## Suggested fix\n\nFor trace checkpoint screenshots, and any default capture of a page with no fixed viewport, use CDP `Page.captureScreenshot` without a `clip`. `captureStableViewport` already does this when `viewportSize()` is null.\n\n====",

Each fix is made in JavaScript, Python and Rust, and the shared parity catalogue and docs are updated with it.\n\nFixes #185\nFixes #179\nFixes #180\nFixes #181\nFixes #183\n\n#181 and #183 are tracking issues. Their only requirement is to resolve #179 and #180 (and, for #183, #181) in one pull request, and this PR does that.\n\n## #179: Chrome for Testing by default, with no infobar and no keychain prompts\n\n| Requested in #179 | Implementation | Tests |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| `resolveLaunchExecutable()` starts Chrome for Testing by default, not the user's Google Chrome | **JS:** `js/src/browser/launch-executable.js` uses Playwright's or Puppeteer's download. Selenium uses one of those, and otherwise asks Selenium Manager for `--force-browser-download`. **Python:** `browser/launch_executable.py` uses Playwright's download, otherwise Selenium Manager's. **Rust:** `launch_executable.rs` takes the path Playwright or Puppeteer reports through Node, otherwise the newest download in the caches. In every language, Google Chrome starts only for `channel: 'chrome'` or an `executablePath`. With no Chrome for Testing installed, the launch fails and the error gives the install command; it never falls back to Google Chrome. | `launch-executable.test.js`, `launcher.test.js`, `webdriver.test.js`, `test_issue_179_chrome_for_testing.py`, `test_launch_browser.py`, `launch_executable_tests.rs`, `engine_launch_tests.rs` |\n| Default restriction `no-chrome-for-testing-infobar` (`--test-type=gpu`) for Chrome for Testing | New restriction and a new `chrome-for-testing` preset in the shared `launch-restrictions.json`. `defaultRestrictionsFor(path, requested)` / `default_restrictions_for` applies the preset only when `isChromeForTesting(path)` matches. Any other browser keeps the command line a person would type. `defaultRestrictions: []` turns the preset off. The session reports what was added as `defaultRestrictions`, and `measureParity()` counts those switches as requested. | Same unit suites, plus `parity.test.js`, `real-browser.test.js` and `real_browser_tests.rs` |\n| `--use-mock-keychain` by default for Chrome for Testing | Part of the same preset. Profile migration (`migrateFrom`) now encrypts with the key of the browser that actually starts: Chromium's fixed mock key, or Chrome for Testing's own \"Chromium Safe Storage\" entry. Before, it used Google Chrome's key, so migrated passwords and cookies did not decrypt. | `os-crypt-keys.test.js`, `test_os_crypt_keys.py`, `rust/src/browser/migration/tests/os_crypt_keys.rs` |\n| Tests for each | `js/tests/e2e/chrome-for-testing.e2e.test.js` starts each JS engine headfully. It reads `chrome://version` to check the executable and both switches. It also measures that the window launched with `defaultRestrictions: []` is taller by the infobar's height. The `Browser Parity` workflow now installs each engine's Chrome for Testing and runs this suite. | CI `Engine lifecycle suites (real Chrome)` |\n\nProblems found and fixed along the way:\n\n- **ChromeDriver version.** Selenium resolved ChromeDriver for the installed Google Chrome, and that driver refuses Chrome for Testing. This affected JS real launches and hand-off reattach, Python real launches, and Rust/fantoccini. The driver is now resolved for the browser that was started (Selenium Manager `--browser-path` / `binary_location`). A `chromedriver` on `PATH` is never used for Chrome for Testing.\n- **Linux sandbox.** On Ubuntu 23.10+ (including `ubuntu-24.04` runners), Chrome for Testing has no AppArmor profile and aborts with \"No usable sandbox!\". The library does **not** add `--no-sandbox` by itself, to keep the command line honest. Instead:\n  - [`docs/chrome-for-testing.md`](docs/chrome-for-testing.md) documents the host fixes;\n  - the engine-suites CI job runs `sysctl kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=0`.\n\nDocs: [`docs/chrome-for-testing.md`](docs/chrome-for-testing.md) (new), `docs/feature-parity.md`, `docs/quiet-chrome.md`, and the three READMEs.\n\n## #180: trace and default screenshots are taken without a `clip`\n\n- **Cause.** Trace checkpoint screenshots used the engine's `page.screenshot()`. For the viewport, Playwright sends `Page.captureScreenshot` with a `clip`, and Chrome emulates that size while it captures. A window resized during the capture can stay drawn at the old size.\n- **Fix.** Trace checkpoints, and default captures of a page that has no fixed viewport, now send CDP `Page.captureScreenshot` without a `clip`. This is in `js/src/traces/recorder.js`, `js/src/capture/screenshot.js`, `python/.../capture.py`, `python/.../traces/engine.py`, `rust/src/capture.rs` and `rust/src/traces/page.rs`.\n- **Tests:**\n  - `js/tests/unit/traces/issue-180-screenshots.test.js`, `python/tests/unit/traces/test_issue_180_screenshots.py` and the Rust stub-engine tests assert that no `clip` is sent.\n  - `experiments/issue-180/resize-during-screenshot.mjs` reproduces the resize race against a real browser.\n\n## How to reproduce\n\n- **#179:** on `main`, run `launchBrowser({ engine: 'playwright' })` on a machine with Google Chrome installed. It starts `/Applications/Google Chrome.app` (or `/usr/bin/google-chrome`). Now it starts `chrome-*/chrome` from the Playwright cache, and `chrome://version` shows `--test-type=gpu --use-mock-keychain`. `experiments/issue-179/` holds the probes.\n- **#180:** run `node experiments/issue-180/resize-during-screenshot.mjs`.\n\n## CI fixes needed for this PR (these also fail on `main`)\n\n- **Security:** `chore(deps)` takes the rustls-webpki, launch-editor and markdown-it advisories that were published on 2026-10-20.\n- **CI Workflow Policy:** zizmor's `ref-version-mismatch` fired at `safari.yml:79` because upstream moved `v2` of `Swatinem/rust-cache`. The comment now names the exact version the SHA points to, `v2.9.2`.\n- **Broken Link Checker:** `chromium.googlesource.com` answered 503 and then let the re-check time out. A 5xx followed by a timeout is now reported as transient, not gone. Test: \"does not fail for a host that answered 5xx and then timed out\".\n\n## CodeQL notes\n\nCodeQL flags `rust/hard-coded-cryptographic-value` at `rust/src/browser/migration/os_crypt_keys.rs:173,175` and in its tests. The flagged strings are `mock_password` and `peanuts`. These are Chromium's public, fixed passwords for the mock keychain and the Linux basic store, not secrets. `main` uses the same constants in `browser_cookies.rs` and `os_crypt_keys.rs`, and the alerts on those lines (for example #35, #67 and #68) are dismissed as false positives. These new alerts should be dismissed the same way.\n\n## Local checks\n\n- **JS:** `npm test`, `npm run lint`, `npm run format:check`, `npm run check:duplication`, and the changeset validation.\n- **Python:** `ruff check`, `ruff format --check`, `mypy src`, and the pytest unit suite.\n- **Rust:** `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -Dwarnings`, `cargo test`, and the file-size check.\n- **Repo:** file line limits, `generate-feature-parity.mjs --check`, actionlint, and zizmor.\n\nRelease notes:\n\n- `js/.changeset/chrome-for-testing-default.md` (minor)\n- `python/changelog.d/179.*.md` and `180.fixed.md`\n- `rust/changelog.d/20261021_160000_chrome_for_testing_default.md` (minor)\n"

This is in `js/src/traces/recorder.js`, `js/src/capture/screenshot.js`, `python/.../capture.py`, `python/.../traces/engine.py`, `rust/src/capture.rs` and `rust/src/traces/page.rs`.\n- **Tests:**\n  - `js/tests/unit/traces/issue-180-screenshots.test.js`, `python/tests/unit/traces/test_issue_180_screenshots.py` and the Rust stub-engine tests assert that no `clip` is sent.\n  - `experiments/issue-180/resize-during-screenshot.mjs` reproduces the resize race against a real browser.\n\n## How to reproduce\n\n- **#179:** on `main`, run `launchBrowser({ engine: 'playwright' })` on a machine with Google Chrome installed. It starts `/Applications/Google Chrome.app` (or `/usr/bin/google-chrome`). Now it starts `chrome-*/chrome` from the Playwright cache, and `chrome://version` shows `--test-type=gpu --use-mock-keychain`. `experiments/issue-179/` holds the probes.\n- **#180:** run `node experiments/issue-180/resize-during-screenshot.mjs`.\n\n## CI fixes needed for this PR (these also fail on `main`)\n\n- **Security:** `chore(deps)` takes the rustls-webpki, launch-editor and markdown-it advisories that were published on 2026-10-20.\n- **CI Workflow Policy:** zizmor's `ref-version-mismatch` fired at `safari.yml:79` because upstream moved `v2` of `Swatinem/rust-cache`. The comment now names the exact version the SHA points to, `v2.9.2`.\n- **Broken Link Checker:** `chromium.googlesource.com` answered 503 and then let the re-check time out. A 5xx followed by a timeout is now reported as transient, not gone. Test: \"does not fail for a host that answered 5xx and then timed out\".\n\n## CodeQL notes\n\nCodeQL flags `rust/hard-coded-cryptographic-value` at `rust/src/browser/migration/os_crypt_keys.rs:173,175` and in its tests. The flagged strings are `mock_password` and `peanuts`. These are Chromium's public, fixed passwords for the mock keychain and the Linux basic store, not secrets. `main` uses the same constants in `browser_cookies.rs` and `os_crypt_keys.rs`, and the alerts on those lines (for example #35, #67 and #68) are dismissed as false positives. These new alerts should be dismissed the same way.\n\n## Local checks\n\n- **JS:** `npm test`, `npm run lint`, `npm run format:check`, `npm run check:duplication`, and the changeset validation.\n- **Python:** `ruff check`, `ruff format --check`, `mypy src`, and the pytest unit suite.\n- **Rust:** `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -Dwarnings`, `cargo test`, and the file-size check.\n- **Repo:** file line limits, `generate-feature-parity.mjs --check`, actionlint, and zizmor.\n\nRelease notes:\n\n- `js/.changeset/chrome-for-testing-default.md` (minor)\n- `python/changelog.d/179.*.md` and `180.fixed.md`\n- `rust/changelog.d/20261021_160000_chrome_for_testing_default.md` (minor)\n",

Main also has a few things ours lacks (point 7).\n\n**1. fantoccini (chromedriver) with Chrome for Testing — main gets this wrong**\n- **Ours:** `with_engine_defaults` (`rust/src/browser/engine_launch.rs:150`) picks the browser through `bundled_engine_executable`. For fantoccini that calls `DownloadCaches::find_driven` (`launch_executable.rs:253`), which prefers a Selenium, Puppeteer or Playwright download that has a chromedriver of the same release. It then sets `webdriver.driver_executable = matching_chromedriver(&executable)` (`engine_launch.rs:171`, defined at `launch_executable.rs:270`). If no Chrome for Testing is found, the launch fails with the install hint.\n- **Main:** `engine_executable` (`origin/main engine_launch.rs:142`) points chromedriver at the newest cached Chrome for Testing (cache order Playwright, Puppeteer, Selenium; `launch_executable.rs:92`). `driver_executable` is never set, so `webdriver/mod.rs:317` falls back to `\"chromedriver\"` on PATH. That is usually the installed Chrome's driver, a different release, which refuses to start the browser. If nothing is cached it returns `None`, and chromedriver silently starts the installed Google Chrome.\n\n**2. Default executables**\n- **chromiumoxide engine mode — main gets this wrong.** Ours resolves Chrome for Testing from the Playwright, Puppeteer and Selenium caches (`launch_executable.rs:160`) and sets `executable_path`. Main uses `chromiumoxide::detection::default_executable` (`engine_launch.rs:157`), which finds the installed Chrome, and only uses it to choose restrictions. `launch(&effective, None, …)` at line 178 never sets an executable, so chromiumoxide still starts the system Chrome.\n- **Real mode (all engines):** both start Chrome for Testing. Main does it in `resolve_default_launch_executable`; ours in `resolve_launch_executable`. Same.\n- **Playwright/Puppeteer engine mode:** both let the engine start its own Chrome for Testing and look it up only to choose restrictions. Same.\n\n**3. Password migration — main lacks this**\n- **Ours:** `migration_target` (`real_browser.rs:383`) sets the target browser to `\"chromium\"` for Chrome for Testing (line 389), because its key is \"Chromium Safe Storage\". It sets `target_keystore` (line 666) through `target_keystore_for` (`os_crypt_keys.rs:141`): `--use-mock-keychain` on macOS or `--password-store=[REDACTED] on Linux means `Mock`. The mock keystore uses `mock_password` / `peanuts` (`os_crypt_keys.rs:173`), the macOS tag is fixed to `v10`, and the `passwords.rs:[REDACTED] / `firefox.rs` prefix defaults are corrected (v11 only on Linux).\n- **Main:** `migrate_options.target_browser = browser_channel()`, which is `\"chrome\"` (`real_browser.rs:650`). It uses the OS keystore and keeps `prefix: \"v11\"` for macOS (`os_crypt_keys.rs:136`). With the default mock keychain, passwords migrated into Chrome for Testing would be encrypted with the wrong key.\n\n**4. `default_restrictions`, result reporting, parity, exports**\n- The `LaunchOptions` and `RealBrowserOptions` fields and builders, `LaunchResult.default_restrictions`, and the `with_default_restrictions` merge are the same.\n- Parity counting is the same logic. Ours moves it into `requested_args_for` (`parity/mod.rs:124`) and adds a unit test; main has it inline at `parity/mod.rs:149`.\n- **Exports:**\n  - Main lacks `CHROME_FOR_TESTING_PRESET` and `resolve_launch_executable` at the crate root. Ours exports both (`lib.rs:109`); main exports the preset only under `browser::` (`browser/mod.rs:78`).\n  - `is_chrome_for_testing`, `default_restrictions_for` and `chrome_for_testing_restrictions` exist on both. Small signature differences: ours takes `impl AsRef<Path>` and returns `&'static [String]`; main takes `&Path` and returns `Vec`.\n\n**5. `--use-mock-keychain` and restriction names**\n`--use-mock-keychain` is a default for Chrome for Testing on both. `launch-restrictions.json` is identical: `no-chrome-for-testing-infobar` (`--test-type=gpu`), `mock-keychain`, and the preset `\"chrome-for-testing\": [\"no-chrome-for-testing-infobar\",\"mock-keychain\"]`. Same.\n\n**6. #180 (screenshots without clip)**\n`capture.rs`, `core/stub_engine.rs` and `snapshot.rs` are byte-identical. `traces/page.rs` differs only by our `// feature-parity: trace.screenshots@native-typed` tag (around line 229), which main lacks. Same otherwise. Main has a separate changelog fragment for it (`20261021_160500_clipless_screenshots.md`); ours folds it into one fragment.\n\n**7. What main has that ours lacks**\n- Chrome for Testing defaults applied directly in `launch_webdriver`: `WebDriverOptions.default_restrictions`, `capabilities::apply_default_restrictions`, `ManagedWebDriver::default_restrictions()` (`webdriver/capabilities.rs:+100`, `webdriver/mod.rs`). Callers of `launch_webdriver` who skip `launch_browser` get the defaults on main; ours only adds them in `with_engine_defaults`.\n- A separate `rust/src/browser/chrome_for_testing.rs` module with injectable `CacheLocations` (platform, home, env), `find_all` returning every candidate newest first, and 264 lines of tests.\n- The example `rust/examples/chrome_for_testing_default.rs`.\n- Updates to `rust/tests/launch_smoke.rs` and `rust/tests/snapshot.rs`.\n- A longer README section (+51 vs +20 lines)."

The mock keystore uses `mock_password` / `peanuts` (`os_crypt_keys.rs:173`), the macOS tag is fixed to `v10`, and the `passwords.rs:[REDACTED] / `firefox.rs` prefix defaults are corrected (v11 only on Linux).\n- **Main:** `migrate_options.target_browser = browser_channel()`, which is `\"chrome\"` (`real_browser.rs:650`). It uses the OS keystore and keeps `prefix: \"v11\"` for macOS (`os_crypt_keys.rs:136`). With the default mock keychain, passwords migrated into Chrome for Testing would be encrypted with the wrong key.\n\n**4. `default_restrictions`, result reporting, parity, exports**\n- The `LaunchOptions` and `RealBrowserOptions` fields and builders, `LaunchResult.default_restrictions`, and the `with_default_restrictions` merge are the same.\n- Parity counting is the same logic. Ours moves it into `requested_args_for` (`parity/mod.rs:124`) and adds a unit test; main has it inline at `parity/mod.rs:149`.\n- **Exports:**\n  - Main lacks `CHROME_FOR_TESTING_PRESET` and `resolve_launch_executable` at the crate root. Ours exports both (`lib.rs:109`); main exports the preset only under `browser::` (`browser/mod.rs:78`).\n  - `is_chrome_for_testing`, `default_restrictions_for` and `chrome_for_testing_restrictions` exist on both. Small signature differences: ours takes `impl AsRef<Path>` and returns `&'static [String]`; main takes `&Path` and returns `Vec`.\n\n**5. `--use-mock-keychain` and restriction names**\n`--use-mock-keychain` is a default for Chrome for Testing on both. `launch-restrictions.json` is identical: `no-chrome-for-testing-infobar` (`--test-type=gpu`), `mock-keychain`, and the preset `\"chrome-for-testing\": [\"no-chrome-for-testing-infobar\",\"mock-keychain\"]`. Same.\n\n**6. #180 (screenshots without clip)**\n`capture.rs`, `core/stub_engine.rs` and `snapshot.rs` are byte-identical. `traces/page.rs` differs only by our `// feature-parity: trace.screenshots@native-typed` tag (around line 229), which main lacks. Same otherwise. Main has a separate changelog fragment for it (`20261021_160500_clipless_screenshots.md`); ours folds it into one fragment.\n\n**7. What main has that ours lacks**\n- Chrome for Testing defaults applied directly in `launch_webdriver`: `WebDriverOptions.default_restrictions`, `capabilities::apply_default_restrictions`, `ManagedWebDriver::default_restrictions()` (`webdriver/capabilities.rs:+100`, `webdriver/mod.rs`). Callers of `launch_webdriver` who skip `launch_browser` get the defaults on main; ours only adds them in `with_engine_defaults`.\n- A separate `rust/src/browser/chrome_for_testing.rs` module with injectable `CacheLocations` (platform, home, env), `find_all` returning every candidate newest first, and 264 lines of tests.\n- The example `rust/examples/chrome_for_testing_default.rs`.\n- Updates to `rust/tests/launch_smoke.rs` and `rust/tests/snapshot.rs`.\n- A longer README section (+51 vs +20 lines).",

It is\nnever the user's own Google Chrome, so automation does not share an\napplication, a Dock icon or a keychain entry with the browser the person uses\n(issue #179). The installed Google Chrome is started only on request:\n\n| Language   | Chrome for Testing (default)  | The installed Google Chrome                     |\n| ---------- | ----------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |\n| JavaScript | `launchBrowser({ engine })`   | `launchBrowser({ engine, channel: 'chrome' })`  |\n| Python     | `launch_browser(engine=...)`  | `launch_browser(engine=..., channel=\"chrome\")`  |\n| Rust       | `LaunchOptions::playwright()` | `LaunchOptions::playwright().channel(\"chrome\")` |\n\n## Which download each engine uses\n\n| Engine                  | Chrome for Testing it starts                                                                  |\n| ----------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |\n| Playwright (JS, Python) | Playwright's `chromium.executablePath()` / `chromium.executable_path`.                        |\n| Puppeteer (JS)          | Puppeteer's `executablePath()`.                                                               |\n| Selenium (JS)           | Playwright's, then Puppeteer's.                                                               |\n| Selenium (Python)       | Playwright's, else the one Selenium Manager downloads.                                        |\n| Rust engines            | The one Playwright or Puppeteer reports through Node, else the newest in the download caches. |\n\nWhen no engine has one, the launch fails with the command that installs it, or\nsays to pass `channel: 'chrome'`; it never falls back to Google Chrome\nsilently.\n\nSelenium attaches through a ChromeDriver, and ChromeDriver drives only the\nChrome release it was built for. The driver is resolved for the Chrome for\nTesting that was started, through Selenium Manager's `--browser-path` and\n`--skip-driver-in-path`: a `chromedriver` on `PATH`, which belongs to the\ninstalled Google Chrome, is not used for Chrome for Testing, although Selenium\nManager would otherwise return it whatever its release. Rust's fantoccini uses\nthe chromedriver Selenium Manager or `@puppeteer/browsers` downloaded for the\nsame release and prefers a download that has one; Playwright downloads none, so\nwith only Playwright's Chrome for Testing it falls back to `chromedriver` on\n`PATH`, which must then be of the same release (or pass `driver_executable`).\n\n## The Linux sandbox on Ubuntu 23.10 and newer\n\nUbuntu 23.10 and newer restrict the unprivileged user namespaces Chromium's\nsandbox needs (`kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=1`). Google\nChrome's package installs an AppArmor profile that exempts it; Chrome for\nTesting has none, so it exits with \"No usable sandbox!\" and the launch fails\nwith that line in its stderr. Browser Commander does not add `--no-sandbox` on\nits own, because the command line stays the one a person would type. Fix the\nhost the way\n[Chromium describes](https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/docs/security/apparmor-userns-restrictions.md) -\nan AppArmor profile for the Chrome for Testing directory, or\n`sudo sysctl -w kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=0` on a disposable\nCI runner - or pass `args: ['--no-sandbox']` where the sandbox is not wanted.\n\n## Default restrictions: no infobar, no keychain prompt\n\nChrome for Testing shows a \"Chrome for Testing is only for automated testing\"\nbar under the toolbar, and on macOS it asks for the keychain password the first\ntime it encrypts cookies or passwords. A launch of Chrome for Testing therefore\nadds the `chrome-for-testing` preset of\n[launch restrictions](feature-parity.md#launch-command-line-and-opt-in-restrictions):\n\n| Restriction                     | Switch                | Effect                                                                                                                                        |\n| ------------------------------- | --------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |\n| `no-chrome-for-testing-infobar` | `--test-type=gpu`     | Hides the bar. Chromium skips it only for this test type, which also skips the unsupported-flag and other startup infobars, and nothing else. |\n| `mock-keychain`                 | `--use-mock-keychain` | Encrypts with a fixed key instead of a \"Chromium Safe Storage\" keychain entry, so macOS never prompts.                                        |\n\nAny other browser - Google Chrome, Edge, Brave, Chromium - gets no default\nrestriction: its command line stays the one a person would type. The session\nreports what was added as `defaultRestrictions` (`default_restrictions` in\nPython and Rust), and `measureParity()` counts these switches as requested.\n\n`defaultRestrictions: []` opts out, and any other list replaces the preset:\n\n```js\nawait launchBrowser({ engine: 'playwright', defaultRestrictions: [] });\n```\n\n```python\nawait launch_browser(engine=\"playwright\", default_restrictions=[])\n```\n\n```rust\nlaunch_browser(LaunchOptions::playwright().default_restrictions(Vec::<String>::new())).await?;\n```\n\n`isChromeForTesting(path)` / `is_chrome_for_testing(path)` and\n`defaultRestrictionsFor(path, requested)` / `default_restrictions_for(path,\nrequested)` expose the same decision. A path is Chrome for Testing when it is\ninside a `chrome-linux64`, `chrome-win64`, `chrome-win32`, `chrome-mac-x64` or\n`chrome-mac-arm64` directory, inside Selenium Manager's\n`selenium/chrome/<platform>/<version>` cache, or names a\n`Google Chrome for Testing` application.\n\n## Profile migration\n\n`migrateFrom` encrypts passwords and cookies with the key of the browser that\nstarts. With the default `mock-keychain` that is Chromium's fixed mock key;\nwithout it, Chrome for Testing uses its own \"Chromium Safe Storage\" keychain\nitem rather than Google Chrome's \"Chrome Safe Storage\".\n\n## Verifying it\n\n`js/tests/e2e/chrome-for-testing.e2e.test.js` launches each JavaScript engine\nheadfully, reads `chrome://version` to check the executable and both switches,\nand measures that the opt-out window is taller by the infobar. The\n`Browser Parity` workflow installs every engine's Chrome for Testing and runs\nit, alongside the Python and Rust default launches.",
